canonical_statement: The review evaluates recent evidence on vitamin D activity in immune cells and its role in infectious and autoimmune inflammatory diseases.
The authors describe reviewing several recent studies concerning vitamin D mechanisms in immune cells and the role of vitamin D in infectious and autoimmune diseases.
The review states that dendritic cells, monocytes/macrophages, and T and B cells express the vitamin D receptor and CYP27B1, enabling these cells to respond to activated vitamin D.
Active vitamin D is reported to downregulate MHC class II and co-stimulatory molecules including CD40, CD80, and CD86 on dendritic cells.
Activated vitamin D or vitamin D analogues are reported to suppress dendritic-cell IL-12 and IL-23 production and promote expression of IL-10.
Recognition of bacterial, viral, or fungal components by toll-like receptors on monocytes/macrophages is reported to upregulate VDR and CYP27B1 expression.
In monocytes/macrophages, CYP27B1 converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; VDR-RXR signaling then induces antimicrobial peptides including cathelicidin and beta-defensin 2.
The review reports that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D induces NOD2 and promotes DEFB4 transcription through NF-kappaB signaling.
The review reports that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D induces macrophage autophagy and promotes antimicrobial activity through cathelicidin-associated pathways.
Vitamin D signaling is reported to regulate epigenetic programming of monocytes/macrophages during immune challenges, affecting immunological memory and immune-cell subtype differentiation.
T cells are reported to express VDR and CYP27B1, with VDR expression increasing as naive T cells become activated.
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is reported to reduce Th1 differentiation and IL-2, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha secretion while promoting Th2 differentiation and IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10 secretion.
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is reported to inhibit Th17-related cytokine secretion and negatively regulate RORC and the aryl hydrocarbon receptor.
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is reported to promote regulatory T-cell differentiation through induction of IL-10 and FoxP3.
The review reports that B cells express VDR and CYP27B1 and that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D directly suppresses naive B-cell differentiation or maturation to memory B cells and plasma cells.

Figure 1 depicts a proposed monocyte/macrophage pathway in which pathogen-triggered TLR signaling increases VDR and CYP27B1, 25D is converted to 1,25D, and downstream cathelicidin, beta-defensin 2, and autophagy support antimicrobial activity.
The review characterizes vitamin D supplementation for infectious-disease treatment as controversial because clinical study results are conflicting.
The review reports that low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is positively correlated with morbidity from upper respiratory tract infections, including influenza.

population.label: Patients evaluated for upper respiratory tract infections

canonical_statement: The review reports that each 10 nmol/L increase in serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was associated with a 7% decrease in infection risk.

population.label: Participants in the cited study of vitamin D level and infection risk

quantitative_result.effect_measure: relative risk change per 10 nmol/L increase (%)
quantitative_result.original_result_text: in cases with an increase in the serum 1,25D level by 10 nmol/L, the risk of infection decreases by 7%

canonical_statement: In an influenza-infected mouse study summarized by the review, a high-25D diet decreased production of IL-5 and IFN-gamma.
The review reports that an RCT in healthy adults using more than 100,000 IU of vitamin D3 for one month did not decrease upper respiratory tract infection morbidity.
The review reports that vitamin D3 at 300 IU/day for three months decreased upper respiratory tract infection morbidity in Mongolian children.
The review reports that daily vitamin D3 at 4000 IU in immunodeficient patients reduced symptoms, pathogen amount detected in mucus, and antibiotic-treatment duration.

concept.text: Respiratory infection symptoms, mucus pathogen burden, and antibiotic-treatment duration

canonical_statement: The review states that a double-blind trial found a significantly lower influenza A rate with vitamin D3 1200 IU/day, while reporting rates of 18.6% for vitamin D3 and 10.8% for placebo.

population.label: Children in the Urashima double-blind trial

canonical_statement: Using the arm rates printed in the review, the vitamin D3 arm had an influenza A incidence 7.8 percentage points higher than placebo (18.6% vs 10.8%), despite the narrative describing the vitamin D3 rate as lower.

population.label: Children in the Urashima double-blind trial

quantitative_result.effect_measure: absolute risk difference, vitamin D3 minus placebo (percentage points)
quantitative_result.original_result_text: children treated with vitamin D3 (1200 IU/day) had a significantly lower rate of flu type A (18.6%) compared to the placebo group (10.8%)

canonical_statement: The review reports that observational studies found serum vitamin D levels inversely correlated with COVID-19 incidence and severity.
The review proposes that vitamin D may influence COVID-19 through renin-angiotensin-system suppression, increased ACE2 in acute lung injury, and an interferon-mediated antiviral response.
A preclinical study summarized by the review found that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D alleviated lipopolysaccharide-induced acute lung injury through effects on renin and angiotensin II expression.
The review describes a constitutive inhibitory interaction between unbound VDR and STAT1 and suggests that vitamin D deficiency could weaken type I interferon-mediated antiviral responses.
The authors state that vitamin D supplementation may contribute to prevention of severe COVID-19.

The review notes that although vitamin D deficiency is associated with onset or exacerbation of autoimmune disease, whether active vitamin D or supplementation improves autoimmune pathology remains debated.
In rheumatoid arthritis, the review reports an inverse correlation of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D with DAS28, TNF-alpha, and IL-6 and a positive correlation with endothelial function.

concept.text: RA disease activity, inflammatory markers, and endothelial function

canonical_statement: In a study of 645 patients with early rheumatoid arthritis, vitamin D deficiency correlated with more active and severe disease and was suggested as a predictor of disability progression over one year.

concept.text: Disease activity, severity, and one-year disability progression

canonical_statement: The review states that a causal relationship between low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and rheumatoid arthritis activity is difficult to establish because severe disease may reduce sunlight exposure and thereby vitamin D synthesis.
The review reports that the Women’s Health Initiative calcium plus vitamin D trial did not show lower rheumatoid arthritis morbidity in the supplemented group than in placebo.

population.label: Participants in the Women’s Health Initiative Calcium plus Vitamin D trial

canonical_statement: A randomized trial summarized by the review included 150 treatment-naive patients with early rheumatoid arthritis and concluded that weekly vitamin D supplementation of 60,000 IU provided pain relief.

population.label: Treatment-naive early rheumatoid arthritis patients in India

canonical_statement: A meta-analysis of six randomized trials summarized by the review found beneficial effects of adjunctive vitamin D on DAS28 and ESR but not on VAS pain score, swollen-joint count, or CRP.

population.label: Participants in six randomized controlled trials of rheumatoid arthritis

concept.text: DAS28, ESR, VAS pain score, swollen-joint count, and CRP

canonical_statement: In subgroup analysis summarized by the review, vitamin D doses above 50,000 IU/week for more than 12 weeks significantly improved VAS pain score in rheumatoid arthritis.

population.label: Rheumatoid arthritis subgroup receiving higher-dose longer-duration supplementation

exposures.details: more than 50,000 IU/week for more than 12 weeks

canonical_statement: In vitro, the review reports that physiologic 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D combined with corticosteroids additively inhibited TNF-alpha, IL-17, IL-6, and MMP production by synoviocytes cocultured with T cells.

concept.text: TNF-alpha, IL-17, IL-6, and MMP production

canonical_statement: The review reports that VDR-deficient mice developed more severe TNF-alpha-induced arthritis with more macrophages and fibroblasts in affected joints.

concept.text: TNF-alpha-induced arthritis severity and joint inflammatory-cell burden

canonical_statement: In adjuvant-induced arthritis, the review reports that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D did not suppress local inflammatory cytokine production but did suppress cytokines in the spleen.

concept.text: Local and splenic inflammatory cytokine production

canonical_statement: The review reports that patients with systemic lupus erythematosus tend to have low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and that lower serum levels are associated with higher SLE disease activity index scores.
A Chinese study summarized by the review found a possible association between vitamin D insufficiency and systemic lupus erythematosus flare severity.

population.label: Chinese patients with systemic lupus erythematosus

canonical_statement: In MRL/lpr lupus mice, one study summarized by the review found that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D improved skin lesions but did not improve renal lesions.
A separate murine lupus study summarized by the review found that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D improved renal lesions, contrasting with the renal finding reported in another model study.
The review reports that treating monocytes from patients with SLE using 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or an analogue decreased antibody production, particularly antinuclear antibodies produced by B cells.

population.label: Monocytes from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus

canonical_statement: The review states that consensus on vitamin D supplementation in systemic lupus erythematosus had not been established.

The review reports that serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D are lower in patients with multiple sclerosis than in healthy volunteers and that serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is associated with disease activity and severity.

population.label: Patients with multiple sclerosis and healthy volunteers

concept.text: Multiple sclerosis disease activity and severity

canonical_statement: A case-control study of US soldiers summarized by the review identified 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency as a risk factor for multiple sclerosis in Caucasians.
The review states that a causal relationship between vitamin D deficiency and multiple sclerosis is difficult to establish.

In the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model, the review reports that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D given before induction prevented disease onset and treatment after induction inhibited disease progression.

Figure 2 presents a proposed EAE mechanism in which 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D suppresses dendritic-cell maturation and IL-12, reduces Th1 proliferation, promotes Th2/Treg differentiation, suppresses TNF-alpha, and promotes IL-10 or TGF-beta.

A clinical study summarized by the review found that vitamin D3 at 50,000 IU every 5 days for three months significantly improved mental state versus placebo in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
The review links vitamin D deficiency with autoimmune endocrine disorders including Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison disease, and Graves disease.
The review reports associations of VDR polymorphisms with autoantibody production and disease susceptibility and of CYP27B1 polymorphism with Addison disease.

population.label: Populations evaluated for autoimmune endocrine disease susceptibility

concept.text: Autoantibody production and autoimmune endocrine disease susceptibility

canonical_statement: The review states that the effectiveness of vitamin D supplementation for preventing progression of the autoimmune endocrine disorders discussed had not been established.

The authors conclude that vitamin D acts directly on immune cells and that vitamin D deficiency is related to infectious-disease morbidity and the onset or progression of autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis.
The authors conclude that vitamin D supplementation has been used to prevent or treat inflammatory diseases but that its effectiveness remains unclear.
The authors call for further study to define disease-specific vitamin D activation mechanisms and establish appropriate treatment strategies.
The authors report that no funding was received for the manuscript.
The article reports that the data availability statement is not applicable.
The authors declare no conflict of interest.
